overview:
Eswatini, known until 2018 as Swaziland, is a small landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, tucked between South Africa and Mozambique. It is smaller than New Jersey but rises from hot lowland bush in the east to cool green mountains in the west. The country has two capitals: Mbabane, where the government offices are, and Lobamba, the royal and traditional capital, home to the parliament and the residence of the Queen Mother.

About 1.2 million people live in Eswatini, almost all of them Swazi. Swazi, also called siSwati, and English are the official languages. Eswatini is the last absolute monarchy in Africa: the king, Mswati III, appoints the prime minister and can overrule parliament, and political parties are not allowed to contest elections. Many Swazis are proud of their traditions and royal ceremonies, while others have protested for democracy. People farm sugarcane, corn, and cattle, work in forestry and textiles, or commute to jobs in South Africa. Wildlife reserves and craft markets draw visitors.
landAndNature: Eswatini is small but varied. The western Highveld is a land of misty mountains, waterfalls, and pine plantations, with Emlembe peak reaching 1,862 meters; the Malolotja reserve there has one of the oldest known rocks on Earth and ancient iron and ochre mines at Ngwenya. The central Middleveld is rolling farmland where most people live. The eastern Lowveld is hot, dry savanna of thorn trees and sugarcane fields, sheltered by the Lubombo Mountains along the Mozambican border. Rivers such as the Komati and Great Usutu cut across the country. Hlane Royal National Park protects lions, elephants, and white rhinos, and Mkhaya reserve shelters rare black rhinos, while Mlilwane is famous for zebras and blue cranes.
peopleAndCulture: Swazi culture centers on the monarchy, clans, and cattle, which are still a measure of wealth. Every year tens of thousands of young men gather for Incwala, the sacred first-fruits ceremony, and unmarried girls in beaded skirts and tassels dance for the Queen Mother at Umhlanga, the Reed Dance, one of Africa's largest cultural events. Traditional dress of bright cloth wraps and animal-skin skirts is worn on special occasions. Corn is the staple, eaten as a stiff porridge with beans, pumpkin, sour milk, or meat stew. Most Swazis are Christian, often blending church with ancestor traditions. Soccer is the top sport, and Swazi crafts such as glassblowing, batik cloth, and woven sisal baskets are sold worldwide.
history: Stone Age hunters and later Bantu-speaking farmers lived here for thousands of years. In the 1700s and 1800s the Dlamini clan under kings Sobhuza I and Mswati II united smaller chiefdoms into the Swazi nation, defending it from Zulu raids; the country is named after Mswati II. Boer and British settlers took much of the land in the late 1800s, and Britain made Swaziland a protectorate in 1903. King Sobhuza II ruled for 82 years, the longest reign of any monarch in recorded history, guiding the country to independence on September 6, 1968 and then suspending the constitution in 1973 to rule directly. His son Mswati III became king in 1986. In 2018 the king renamed the country Eswatini, meaning land of the Swazis. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were put down by force.
funFacts: King Sobhuza II reigned for 82 years, from 1899 to 1982, the longest verified reign of any monarch in history.
The Ngwenya mine in Eswatini was dug by humans about 43,000 years ago, making it one of the oldest mines in the world.
The country changed its name from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018 partly because people kept confusing it with Switzerland.
Eswatini has two capital cities: Mbabane for the government and Lobamba for the king and parliament.
The Umhlanga Reed Dance draws tens of thousands of girls and young women who present reeds to the Queen Mother.
